sections:
**Alignment solves “answering well”, not “being able to answer”.**

After SFT the model answers in format, but there is no signal for “which answer is better, where the line is crossed”.
The original recipe for this step is InstructGPT's (arXiv 2203.02155) RLHF:
humans rank answers, a reward model is trained, then PPO makes the language model court that reward model.

Humans do not score directly; they compare pairs: of two answers to the same prompt, which is better.
Anthropic's HH data (arXiv 2204.05862) splits the axes into helpful and harmless.
The reward model learns this ranking tendency and emits a scalar score.

The trap practitioners must watch: the reward model is a proxy metric, not goodness itself.
It can be gamed — longer, more confident, model-essay-like answers score higher.
“Length bias” is a side effect repeatedly acknowledged in RLHF-era papers.

InstructGPT's RL stage keeps four models resident at once:
the policy being trained, the reference model that keeps it on the rails (KL constraint), the reward model, and the critic.
Memory and compute cost several times SFT, and tuning is touchy (a skewed KL coefficient collapses the run).

LLaMA 2 (arXiv 2307.09288) published both routes side by side:
iterative SFT bootstrapping versus rejection sampling plus PPO, each winning on different evaluations.
The authors themselves declared no outright winner; this site reports it as stated.

DPO's (arXiv 2305.18290) derivation shows the optimal policy has a closed form,
so preference pairs can feed a classification-style loss directly — no reward model to train, no RL to run.
Memory drops back to SFT scale, the code is dozens of lines.

Zephyr (arXiv 2310.16944) took a 7B model to the front of its size class at the time using public data,
proving the route is community-reproducible.

The cost too: DPO is sensitive to the distribution of preference pairs, and offline training easily “overfits the ranking style”;
online RLHF keeps sampling fresh answers, so the signal stays fresher.
Published head-to-head conclusions between the two routes are unstable and data-dependent.
This site adjudicates neither — it records each mechanism and its published limits.

Constitutional AI (arXiv 2212.08073) uses a written set of principles to make the model criticise and
revise itself, then lets models prefer models. Human ranking retreats to a calibration role.

Open-weight families' post-training routinely mixes this route in —
the bottleneck that caps scale moves from compute to annotation.

The “alignment tax” is the score a model can lose on original-task evaluations after alignment.
The InstructGPT paper itself observed GPT-3 regressing on some public benchmarks because of alignment.

Sycophancy is the mirror image of preference data:
humans favour answers that agree with them, so the reward model learns to agree.

Neither is rumour — both are side effects admitted in the papers themselves.
When reading any model's official benchmarks, remember:
post-alignment scores mix “a style that pleases the grader” with “actual capability”.

The one-page explainers live on the Learn site: [three-stage training](https://learn.specul.com/term/训练三阶段/)
and [preference alignment](https://learn.specul.com/term/偏好对齐/).

This guide covers the cost structure of four resident models, how a proxy metric can be gamed,
and the sources behind the alignment tax and sycophancy — the traps practitioners watch, which an explainer page cannot hold.
